The match starts. The other team is tall, and fast too. The first goal is theirs. Mum says, "It doesn't matter, there's still time."

In the end it's one-all. My brother is a bit tired, but happy. In the evening we go to a restaurant together. My brother eats lots of rice.

Grandpa told me their team wasn't big and had no money. They bought their own boots, and the pitch was a tiny patch of ground. But everyone was serious and trained every day after work.
"In our best year we beat every factory team in the city," Grandpa said, laughing. "That night we all went out to eat, drank a lot and sang all night."

I asked Grandpa, "Would you like to watch a match at the stadium again?" He said, "I'd like to, but I can't walk that far." I thought for a moment and said, "I'll take you! We'll drive, and I'll push your wheelchair."
The next Saturday Grandpa and I went to the stadium. He wore his old shirt, and lots of people looked at him. A young man came over and said, "Grandpa, your shirt is so cool!"
During the match Grandpa kept shouting and laughing, as if he'd become young again. On the way home he held my hand and said, "Thank you, child. Today was the happiest day I've had in years."

translations: Before coming to Beijing I'd already decided: I had to go to the Great Wall. I'd looked at lots of photos online, blue sky, long walls, really beautiful.
That morning I got up at six. The sky was a bit overcast, but I thought it probably wouldn't rain. I took a two-hour bus ride to the foot of the Great Wall.
I started climbing. The Great Wall was much harder to climb than I'd imagined; some parts were very high, some very narrow. After half an hour I was exhausted.
Just then it started to rain. At first it was light, then it got heavier and heavier. I hadn't brought an umbrella, and my clothes were soon soaked. I stood in a little watchtower, feeling fed up.
There was an old man in the watchtower too. He saw me and said with a smile, "Young man, first time here?" I said, "Yes, but the weather is awful."
The old man said, "I've sold water here for twenty years. The Wall is beautiful on sunny days, and beautiful on rainy days too; it's just that few people see it." He gave me a cup of hot tea.

I drank the tea and looked outside. In the rain the Great Wall ran on over the mountains with no end in sight. The mountains were covered in white mist, like a Chinese painting. I took out my phone and took lots of photos.
Half an hour later the rain stopped. I said goodbye to the old man and kept climbing. I didn't see a blue sky that day, but I saw a Great Wall few people get to see.
Now my favourite photo on my phone is the Great Wall in the rain that day. Every time I see it, I remember that cup of hot tea and what the old man said.

translations: Near our university there's a very old street, and at the end of it is a tiny tailor's shop. There's no sign outside, just an old pair of scissors hanging by the door.

The first time I went in was because I'd bought a very long pair of trousers at a second-hand market and wanted them shortened. The shop was dark, with fabric everywhere, and an old master with completely white hair was sewing.

The old tailor's surname was Chen, and he'd been a tailor for fifty years. He looked at my trousers, felt the fabric and said, "These aren't ordinary trousers. They're made in Japan, and the fabric is excellent. It'd be a shame to cut them."
I was surprised and asked how he knew. Master Chen smiled: "Fifty years in, you can tell by touch. Look at the thread here: every stitch is neat. Few people make things like this now."
Instead of cutting the trousers, he sewed a small hem on the inside. "This way, if you want them long later, just unpick the thread." I tried them on; the length was perfect.

After that I often went to Master Chen's shop. Sometimes to alter clothes, sometimes just to drink tea and hear his old stories. He said that in the eighties everyone had their clothes made, and there was a long queue outside his shop every day.
"Now everyone buys cheap clothes at the mall and throws them away after a year," Master Chen said a little sadly. "Clothes are like people: you have to spend time with them before you get attached."

Last month I heard the street was going to be demolished. I went to find Master Chen straight away. He was packing up and seemed calm. He gave me a small pair of scissors and said, "From now on, learn to alter your own clothes."
Now those scissors sit on my desk. Every time I buy an old piece of clothing, I look carefully at its thread and fabric first, as if Master Chen were still beside me.

translations: Last year my cousin opened a bubble tea shop in the university district. When it opened business was great, with a long queue every day. But six months later she called me, sounding exhausted.
"You study accounting, can you look at my books?" she said. "The shop's busy every day, but at the end of the month there's never enough money."
At the weekend I went to her shop. Her books were a mess: some in a notebook, some on her phone, and some not recorded at all. It took me two full days to sort out six months of accounts.

The problems soon became clear. One: rent was too high, a third of revenue. Two: she prepared lots of fresh fruit every day, but it didn't sell by evening and had to be thrown away. Three: the delivery platform took a twenty percent fee.
My cousin looked at the spreadsheet I'd made and said nothing for ages. Finally she said, "So I've been busy all this time, but not making money."

We came up with a few ideas together. Instead of preparing a whole day's fruit at once, she'd prep it three times a day. She cut a few slow-selling drinks from the menu. She also started selling homemade cakes, because cakes have a higher margin than bubble tea.

Most importantly, I made her a simple spreadsheet so she could spend ten minutes on the books after closing each day. At first she found it a hassle, but then she found that seeing the numbers every day gave her real peace of mind.
Three months later my cousin called again. This time she sounded happy: "We finally made a profit this month!" She said she'd treat me to a year of bubble tea.
I laughed: "Then I'm going to get fat." After hanging up I felt, for the first time, that the accounting in my textbooks really could help someone make their dream come true.

translations: After graduating I joined a small animation studio. At the interview I showed them my portfolio. The boss looked at it for a long time and said just one thing: "Start tomorrow."
On my first day I discovered that reality was nothing like I'd imagined. I thought I'd be designing characters straight away; instead I was assigned to draw in-betweens.

In-betweens are all the frames that fill the gap between two key poses drawn by a key animator. If someone turns their head, the key animator draws only the start and end; the dozen or so frames in between are drawn by newcomers like me.
The work was incredibly tedious and exhausting. I drew over a hundred frames a day, earning less than ten kuai per frame. Finishing at midnight was normal, and I often worked weekends.
For a while I really wanted to quit. I began to wonder whether I actually liked making animation, or just liked watching it.

Right then, a veteran key animator at the studio noticed me. His name was Mr Lin, and he'd been in the industry thirty years. He went through my drawings one by one and pointed out many problems I'd never considered.
"Your drawing is clean, but it has no weight," he said. "When someone jumps down, their clothes, hair and body all land at different moments. Observe life first, then animate."
From that day, every time I took the metro I watched people: how they walked, how they turned, how their bags swung. My notebook filled with sketches. Slowly my in-betweens came to life.

Two years later I was allowed to draw key animation for the first time. It was a shot of a little girl running in the rain, only three seconds long. On the night it aired, I stared at the screen, watching it again and again.
The end credits were long, and my name was near the end, so small it was almost unreadable. But to me those were the best three seconds in the world.

translations: In 1981 two Japanese designers showed in Paris for the first time. In a Paris where glamour and sex appeal were the mainstream, their clothes were almost all black: loose, tattered, even with irregular holes.
The next day the French press was scathing. Some even called the show "Hiroshima chic", saying the clothes looked as if they'd survived a disaster.

Within a few years black had become shorthand for avant-garde fashion. From Antwerp to New York, many important later designers have openly said they were deeply influenced by that show.

Looking back today, the clothes that were mocked back then have become classics that major museums compete to collect. On the second-hand market an original piece from the eighties often sells for dozens of times its original price.
This history often makes me think: things of real value may always make people uncomfortable when they first appear.

translations: Last spring I spent a week on a tea mountain in Yunnan, living with a family that has made Pu'er tea for four generations. The host, Yan Wen, is from the Blang ethnic group.

Every day at five in the morning, before the mist had cleared, Yan Wen took us up the mountain to pick tea. He said the best spring tea comes in just twenty-odd days around Qingming; miss it and you wait another year.

Picking tea looks simple but takes real care: only pick one bud and two leaves, with a light touch, never pinching with your nails, or the leaves turn black. I picked all morning and managed less than a fifth of what he did.

In the afternoon came the kill-green and rolling. A huge iron wok was scorching hot, and Yan Wen tossed the leaves in it with his bare hands, so fast I couldn't follow. The whole courtyard smelled of fresh tea.

In the evening the family sat round the fire pit drinking tea and chatting. Yan Wen's father said tea used to fetch no price, and young people all left to work elsewhere. Only in recent years, as the mountain became famous, have they slowly come back.

The day I left, Yan Wen gave me a cake of tea he'd pressed himself, with my name and the year written on it. He said, "Pu'er gets better with age. Drink it in ten years and you'll remember this mountain."

translations: The summer we graduated, my university roommate A-Kai and I decided to drive the Sichuan–Tibet highway. From Chengdu to Lhasa is over two thousand kilometres; with detours, we drove nearly three thousand in the end.

Before we left almost the whole family was against it. Mum reminded me again and again on the phone about the dangers of altitude sickness, and Dad worried we didn't have enough driving experience. To reassure them, we started getting fit a month ahead and even took a basic car maintenance course.

The first few days went fairly smoothly. The view outside gradually changed from the green of the Sichuan Basin to high mountains and gorges. After Kangding the altitude rose rapidly; for the first time I had headaches and trouble breathing, and barely slept all night.

On day four we hit real trouble. Heavy rain the night before had caused a landslide, and the road ahead was completely blocked. Hundreds of vehicles formed a long line, and no one knew how long we'd wait.

As everyone waited anxiously, I noticed people in the line starting to help each other. A Tibetan man took hot water to every car, some young cyclists shared their biscuits with families travelling with children, and someone got out a guitar and started singing by the road.

We waited eleven hours in all. The moment the road was cleared, the whole line erupted in horns, as if celebrating a victory. That night I wrote in my diary: "The most beautiful sight may not be the snow mountains, but kindness between strangers."

The road ahead grew more dangerous, and more beautiful. We crossed several passes around five thousand metres, saw lakes so blue they looked unreal, and were held up for half an hour on the grassland by a huge herd of yaks.

One night we stayed in a little village of only a dozen or so households. The old lady who ran the guesthouse spoke no Mandarin; she just smiled and poured us butter tea. Using a translation app, we chatted haltingly all evening.

On day fifteen we finally reached Lhasa. Standing in front of the Potala Palace, A-Kai suddenly said, "Actually, where we ended up doesn't matter any more." I knew what he meant. On the way we hadn't learned how to drive; we'd learned how to stay patient amid uncertainty.

Back home we both soon started work: squeezing onto the metro, meetings, overtime. But whenever I'm under pressure, I think of that road blocked for eleven hours, of that cup of hot water and that song, and tell myself: wait a little longer, the road always opens again.

stories.title_en: Grandma learns to use a smartphone
translations: The year of the pandemic, my 78-year-old grandma suddenly found she could barely do anything without a smartphone: scanning a code to enter the supermarket, booking to see a doctor, even paying by phone to buy vegetables.
So when I went home for Spring Festival I bought her a new phone and decided to teach her. It turned out to be much harder than I'd imagined.

Things we take for granted were all puzzles for her. She couldn't tell "tap" from "long press" and often deleted apps by accident. The text was too small to read and the sound too quiet to hear; every step had to be repeated several times.

Once I couldn't help getting a bit impatient and said, "I've already shown you this three times." Grandma froze for a second, then said quietly, "Sorry, I'm old, my brain doesn't work well any more." In that moment I felt deeply ashamed.

So I tried a different approach: I drew every step on a big sheet of paper, numbered in red pen, and stuck it by her bed. I also set the font to the largest size and put the few apps she uses on the first screen.

Now Grandma can video-call and send voice messages with ease, and even posts stickers in the family group chat. A few days ago she sent me a message: "Grandson, it's getting cold, wrap up warm." Followed by a big smiley face.

translations: In my sixth year renting in Shanghai, my landlord suddenly told me the flat was being sold and he hoped I'd move out within a month. After hanging up, I sat on the sofa staring into space for a long time.

I found this old one-bedroom flat just after graduating. On my modest salary, I viewed over twenty flats with an agent, and chose this one simply because from the balcony you could see a huge plane tree.

Over six years this flat witnessed many of the important moments of my life. Here I stayed up late studying for the CPA exam, got my first promotion letter, and spent, alone, the hardest winter after a breakup.

Only when packing did I realise how much stuff I'd accumulated. Deep in a drawer was a cinema ticket stub from the first film I saw with my ex; on top of the wardrobe was a box of university textbooks, their pages covered in dense notes.

I set myself a rule: anything unused for over a year either gets given away or thrown out. But when it came to it, every item I picked up made me hesitate for ages. In the end I tucked that ticket stub into a book and took it with me.

The night before the move, my downstairs neighbour, Auntie Wang, knocked on the door. She was holding a bowl of freshly made wontons and said, "These past few years you fixed my pipes and picked up my parcels. At your new place, make sure you eat properly." As I took the bowl, a lump rose in my throat.

The new flat is closer to work, newer and brighter. The first night I lay in an unfamiliar bed listening to unfamiliar sounds and just couldn't sleep. Outside the window there was no plane tree, only rows of identical tower blocks.

For a while I often took the long way home after work, back past the old building, and looked up at that balcony. One day I saw a new pot of flowers on it; the light was on, and someone was moving about inside.
In that moment I suddenly let go. A home doesn't belong to anyone; it just keeps us company along part of the way. What matters isn't holding on to it, but remembering who you became there.

On the metro home I messaged Auntie Wang and invited her to dinner at my new place the next weekend. She quickly replied with a big "OK". Looking at my phone screen, for the first time the new flat didn't feel quite so strange.

translations: Many people think that as long as a company makes a profit, it won't go under. In fact, lots of businesses are still profitable on paper when they collapse; the real cause is that their cash flow dried up.
For example: you sell a batch of goods at a handsome profit, but the customer won't pay for six months. Meanwhile, every month you have to pay wages, rent and your suppliers.

That's why accounting teachers often say, "Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact." To judge whether a company is healthy, don't just look at the income statement; look even more at the cash flow statement.

translations: My cousin studied marketing at university. After graduating, instead of joining a company, she started livestreaming online to sell specialities from her home town: cured pork, rice wine and handmade chilli sauce.

For the first three months each stream had only a few dozen viewers, and she couldn't sell ten orders a night. She talked to her phone for four or five hours a day until her voice went, yet her income wasn't even enough for rent.

The turning point came by accident. One day during a stream, her grandma suddenly walked into shot and, in a thick dialect, taught viewers how to make cured pork. Unexpectedly, the clip was edited and went viral; overnight she gained fifty thousand followers.

My cousin realised that what viewers really wanted wasn't a sales pitch but real life. So she changed strategy: talk less about prices, tell more stories, and point the camera at the village fields, the stoves and the old people's craft.

Now she has built a small team of six and signed a long-term purchasing agreement with the village cooperative. Last year her shop's sales passed three million yuan, and it helped over a dozen village households earn more.

But my cousin is clear-headed about it. She says the livestream industry changes too fast; traffic comes quickly and goes just as quickly. She's planning to register her own brand and get her products into supermarkets. As she says, "Traffic is given to you by others. A brand is your own."

translations: Twelve yards, less than eleven metres, yet many players call it the longest walk in the world. In a penalty shoot-out the goalkeeper barely has time to react, so in theory the taker holds an overwhelming advantage; and yet history is full of stars who have regretted a missed penalty for the rest of their lives.

Psychologists' research shows that what decides a penalty is often not technique but pressure. When the kick determines whether the whole match is lost, players' conversion rates drop significantly; when scoring means winning outright, the rate actually goes up. In other words, fear of failure sways performance more than the desire for success.

Interestingly, researchers also found that players who rush at the ball and deliberately avoid the goalkeeper's gaze miss noticeably more often. They seem to want only to end the ordeal as fast as possible, rather than focusing on how to score.

So more and more teams are building mental training into their routine. In training, players simulate jeers, floodlights and fatigue, practising a fixed breathing rhythm and run-up under pressure. Some coaches even have players pause for two seconds before shooting, shifting their attention from "I mustn't miss" to "where am I putting it".

Ultimately, a penalty tests not just technique but your ability to hold a conversation with yourself. Those few seconds on the spot may be the moment where football comes closest to life: no one can carry it for you, and there's no way back.

translations: At the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, Belgium, fashion students are often set an assignment that seems to have nothing to do with clothing: first write a poem, or take a series of photos, then turn the emotion in it into clothes.

This way of teaching is less about training tailors than about training authors. The teachers believe technique can be learned in a few years, but whether a designer has their own language decides how far they'll go.

In the 1980s, six young graduates from here hired a lorry and drove their work to London for a trade show. Their names were long and hard to pronounce, so British journalists simply called them the "Antwerp Six". It was this gamble that turned a port city famed for its diamond trade into a centre of avant-garde fashion almost overnight.

Of course, this model of education is highly controversial. The academy is known for its high drop-out rate; often only a third of a year group makes it to graduation. Some criticise it as too harsh, crushing plenty of talent; others believe it's exactly this pressure that draws out real creativity.

I once asked a friend who studied there what she gained most. She thought for a long time and said, "They made me understand that clothes aren't decoration, they're expression. You can dislike what I make, but you can't fail to see what I'm trying to say."

translations: My grandfather was a tailor at an old, established suit shop in Shanghai all his life. As a child I'd often lean on his workbench watching him mark lines on fabric with chalk and cut along them with scissors; that crisp, decisive sound still echoes in my ears.

His favourite saying was, "Clothes don't mind being old; they mind being neglected." To him, wearing a garment out was no pity; the pity was people throwing it away before they'd had a chance to mend it. His drawer held dozens of colours of thread, and a tin full of all kinds of buttons he'd taken off old clothes over the decades.

When he died I inherited the tin but never knew what to do with it. Until a few years ago, in a little shop in Tokyo, I first saw boro: clothes and quilts that farmers in Japan's Tohoku region, in times of scarcity, stitched together from layer upon layer of scraps.

A blue garment mended at least several hundred times hung in the most prominent spot in the shop. Look closely and every patch's colour and every line of stitching's density differed; clearly it was the work of several generations. The owner told me such pieces are now collected as art, and have even entered European museums.

Standing in front of it, I suddenly thought of my grandfather's tin. On opposite sides of the ocean, in two eras unknown to each other, people had fought waste in the same way: not with slogans, but with patience, stitch by stitch.

After coming home I started learning to mend my own old clothes. At first my stitches were crooked and my patches ugly, but I gradually found the act of mending itself strangely healing. In an age when everything chases "faster, newer", sitting down for two hours to sew up a hole is almost a gentle act of resistance.

I also filmed my mending and posted it online, and to my surprise it struck a chord with lots of young people. Some sent photos of their first mend, some commented that it reminded them of a late grandmother, and a fashion design student told me she planned to make "mending" the theme of her graduate collection.

Of course, I've heard doubts too: what can one person mending a few clothes change? The fashion industry produces tens of millions of tonnes of textile waste every year; individual effort seems insignificant.

I can't argue with that. But perhaps change was never going to happen overnight. My grandfather's lifetime of buttons, the northern farmers' garments sewn over generations: none of them changed the world, yet they let a certain attitude of care be handed down.

Now the tin sits on my workbench. Whenever I can't find the right button, I open it and rummage. Buttons from different eras and different clothes lie quietly together, as if reminding me: as long as someone is willing to care for old things, they never truly lose their value.

translations: If Miyazaki's work has a common motif, it must be flight. Whether it's the little witch delivering parcels on a broomstick, or the engineer designing planes amid war, his characters always seem to be looking for a way to leave the ground.

Yet flight in his stories is never simply romantic. The hero of The Wind Rises devotes his life to designing the most beautiful aeroplane, only to watch helplessly as his life's work is used for war. Beauty and destruction, dreams and their cost, are tangled together under the same sky.

To some extent this contradiction mirrors Miyazaki himself. His father's family factory made parts for fighter planes, yet he is a committed pacifist. He is fascinated by the beauty of machines while remaining deeply wary of technology's misuse.

That's exactly why his work rarely offers black-and-white answers. Villains often have sympathetic reasons, and heroes inevitably make mistakes. What he cares about more is how people stay kind in a complicated world, and how, knowing reality is imperfect, they still choose to live well.

Perhaps that's why many people who saw only the joy of flying in his films as children find themselves in tears at some quiet shot when they rewatch them as adults. The sky is the same sky; what's changed is that we've finally understood its weight.

translations: I arrived in Dunhuang at dusk. Before landing I looked out of the window: the endless Gobi glowed rust-red in the setting sun, and the city looked like a little oasis someone had casually dropped into a sea of sand.

Early the next morning I went to the Mogao Caves. Our guide was a middle-aged woman who'd worked there for over twenty years and spoke in an unhurried way. She told us that to protect the murals, each cave has a strict daily visitor limit; the moisture and carbon dioxide tourists breathe out speed up the flaking of the pigments.

Stepping into a Tang dynasty cave, as the torchlight swept across the walls, flying apsaras with ribbons streaming looked as if they might leap off the wall any second. The guide said most of the painters left no names; they were ordinary artisans who came here, generation after generation, from the Central Plains and the Western Regions over a thousand years ago.

What moved me most was the story of one old man. In the 1940s he gave up a comfortable life studying painting in Paris and came to this desert, where he stayed for half a century. There was no electricity then, winters hit minus twenty, and they lived in converted stables, gradually compiling the damaged murals into volumes by copying and recording them.

On my last evening I climbed Mingsha Mountain. Wind swept over the dunes with a deep hum. Below, the Crescent Moon Spring lay quietly in the middle of the desert; in two thousand years it has never run dry. I suddenly felt that the most precious thing in this land, besides the murals, is the dedication of generation after generation who asked nothing in return.

translations: My father isn't a man of words. Growing up, I almost never heard him say "I love you" or "I'm proud of you". His way of showing care was always surprisingly concrete: a box of apples sent from our home town, a text reminding me to wrap up when the temperature dropped, or a car already filled with petrol when I came home.

When I was young, I resented it. Watching classmates' fathers hug them and take photos at graduation, I wondered more than once why mine couldn't say a bit more. He stood at the very back of the crowd with a slightly wilted bunch of flowers, nodded at me, and that was his congratulations.

Only when I started working myself did I gradually understand how hard things were for him. That year, working in another city, I was hit by a major round of layoffs and was unemployed for six whole months. I didn't dare tell my family and said everything was fine every time I called. But one day twenty thousand kuai suddenly appeared in my bank account, with a transfer note of just four characters: "Don't work too hard."

Later my mother told me that during that time my father searched online every night for news about my industry, and when he saw reports of layoffs he'd smoke alone on the balcony, half a pack at a time. He'd guessed everything, yet asked nothing.

Now that I'm a father myself, I understand that some love is silent not because it's shallow but because it's so heavy that saying it out loud would make it sound flimsy. A few days ago I called him. After talking about the weather and the crops, I hesitated for a long time and finally said, "Dad, thank you." There were a few seconds of silence on the other end, then a slightly hoarse: "Mm."

translations: On Qianmen Street in Beijing there's a cloth-shoe brand founded in the late Qing dynasty. In the 1990s, as trainers and leather shoes became widespread, its sales plummeted; its shops shrank from over a dozen to just one, and at one point it was on the brink of closing.

In 2015 the fifth generation of the founding family took over. She had worked for years at a foreign consultancy, and the first thing she did on taking charge wasn't to launch new products but to spend three months going through thirty years of sales data and customer feedback, one item at a time.

The analysis was surprising: losing old customers was certainly a serious problem, but the real issue was that the brand was practically "invisible" to young people. Many didn't dislike cloth shoes; they simply didn't know anyone still made them by hand.

So she made a few decisions that were quite controversial at the time: keep the traditional thousand-layer sole craft, but boldly launch collaborations with young designers; livestream the whole process of the old masters stitching soles on social media; and invest part of the profits in a training programme for intangible heritage craftspeople.

At first many long-serving staff worried these moves would "ruin the name". But the facts proved that tradition and innovation aren't incompatible. Three years later online sales made up over sixty percent of revenue, and the share of buyers under thirty-five had quadrupled.

Asked why it worked, she said, "The most valuable thing about an old brand isn't the name on the sign, but the reverence for craft behind it. As long as you hold on to that, you needn't fear any change of form."

translations: In my first year in the profession, I was mentored by a partner surnamed Zhou. In his early fifties, grey-haired and unhurried in speech, he was famous throughout the firm for his "sharp eye". It was said he only had to flip through a few pages of financial statements to sniff out what was wrong.

Once we took on a manufacturer preparing to list. Its financials were impeccably good: revenue up over thirty percent three years running, gross margin far above its peers, ample cash reserves. The young people on the team were excited, thinking this would be the smoothest job imaginable.

Mr Zhou, however, spent a whole afternoon in the meeting room looking at the balance sheet. Towards evening he called me over, pointed at the "accounts receivable" and "inventory" lines and asked, "What do you think is wrong with these two numbers?"

I stared at them for ages; they just looked big, and I couldn't say why. Unhurried, he explained: revenue grew thirty percent, but receivables grew eighty percent, meaning more and more sales weren't being collected in cash; and inventory days were getting longer every year, suggesting the products might not really have been sold.
"The income statement can tell a story," he said, "but the balance sheet gives away secrets. If a company really made money, the money has to have gone somewhere."

Over the next two months, following his line of thinking, we checked the contracts, delivery notes and bank receipts of the company's top twenty customers item by item, and even visited several customers' warehouses to count stock in person. The more we dug, the more doubts arose: one customer's registered address was an empty office; some "sold" goods sat untouched in a warehouse the company itself rented.

In the end we confirmed that the company had used related parties to fabricate transactions, inflating revenue by nearly four hundred million yuan over three years. We issued a qualified opinion, and the company's listing plans stalled. Afterwards some colleagues grumbled privately that we'd lost a big client and this year's bonuses were probably gone.
When Mr Zhou heard, he just said calmly, "An auditor's signature is a promise to the millions of investors you'll never see. Sign wrongly once, and no one will ever trust you again."

That night I wrote that sentence on the first page of my notebook. Since then I've handled over a hundred engagements, seen every kind of financial statement, and faced all sorts of pressure, carrot and stick alike. Whenever I waver, I think of that afternoon and Mr Zhou's calm expression as he pointed at those two lines.

Last year Mr Zhou retired. At his farewell party we asked him to leave a few words for the young ones. He thought for a moment and said, "Numbers themselves don't lie; people do. Our job is to guard the last door for everyone who trusts the numbers."
